questions.stem: Which apparatus and procedure is used to determine the melting point of a crystalline substance?

options.A: A volumetric flask filled with a saturated standard solution
options.B: A Woulff's bottle connected to a vacuum pump
options.C: A melting-point capillary tube attached to a thermometer, immersed in a slowly heated oil or water bath
options.D: A Kipp's apparatus with solid and liquid acid chambers

questions.explanation: Melting point determination uses a thin capillary tube containing the solid attached to a thermometer in a heating bath. The sharp MP indicates purity.

questions.stem: A combustion tube for organic analysis must be made of what material?

options.A: Soda-lime glass — transparent and thin-walled
options.B: Polypropylene plastic for broad chemical resistance
options.C: Pyrex (borosilicate) or hard glass — to withstand very high combustion temperatures
options.D: Porcelain — same material as crucibles

questions.explanation: Pyrex/borosilicate glass has very low thermal expansion and can withstand the high temperatures used in organic combustion analysis (600–900°C).

questions.stem: Crucible tongs are used in the chemistry laboratory for which specific operation?

options.A: Handling hot crucibles, evaporating dishes, and other hot porcelain items safely
options.B: Tightening the stopcock of a burette or separating funnel
options.C: Clamping a Liebig condenser to the distillation flask
options.D: Crushing large solid samples before analysis

questions.explanation: Crucible tongs are made of metal and designed to grip the rim of hot crucibles and porcelain ware without burning hands or risking dropping.

questions.stem: What is the function of a delivery tube in a gas preparation experiment?

options.A: To store the prepared gas at elevated pressure
options.B: To absorb moisture and impurities from the prepared gas
options.C: To convey (lead) the prepared gas from the generator to the collection vessel or test reagent
options.D: To measure the rate of gas production in cm³ per minute

questions.explanation: The delivery tube connects the gas generator (flask) to the collection vessel or testing solution, guiding the gas flow through the system.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a pneumatic trough in gas collection?

options.A: To dry the gas using a column of drying agent
options.B: To absorb acidic impurities from the gas stream
options.C: To hold water so that gas can be collected by displacement in an inverted jar
options.D: To measure the volume of gas produced at standard conditions

questions.explanation: The pneumatic trough is filled with water. Gas bubbles up from the delivery tube into the inverted, water-filled gas jar, displacing the water.

questions.stem: The amber (dark brown) reagent bottle is designed for what specific purpose?

options.A: Storing dry solids that readily absorb moisture
options.B: Storing liquid reagents that decompose on exposure to sunlight (e.g. H₂O₂, AgNO₃, iodine solutions)
options.C: Storing concentrated acids that attack ordinary glass
options.D: Collecting and storing gases produced during reactions

questions.explanation: Amber glass blocks UV and visible light that would catalyse the decomposition of light-sensitive reagents like H₂O₂, AgNO₃, and iodine solutions.

questions.stem: A desiccator is used to store substances after drying. What is placed in the base to absorb moisture?

options.A: Concentrated HCl to absorb basic vapours
options.B: Silica gel, CaCl₂, or P₂O₅ — desiccant that absorbs water vapour from the enclosed space
options.C: Activated charcoal to remove organic vapour impurities
options.D: Distilled water to maintain a constant humidity inside

questions.explanation: A desiccator stores hygroscopic substances in a dry environment. Common desiccants: silica gel (mild), CaCl₂, anhydrous CaSO₄, and P₂O₅ (very strong).

questions.stem: The volumetric (standard) flask has a single graduation mark on its narrow neck. What is its specific purpose?

options.A: Heating liquids to boiling point and collecting distillate
options.B: Collecting filtrate during suction filtration
options.C: Preparing a standard solution of a precise, definite volume (e.g. exactly 250.00 cm³)
options.D: Distilling immiscible liquid mixtures at varying pressures

questions.explanation: The volumetric flask's single calibration mark ensures exactly the stated volume when the meniscus is at the mark. Used to prepare standard solutions.

questions.stem: A Buchner flask (side-arm flask) side arm is connected to what during filtration under reduced pressure?

options.A: A Liebig condenser for cooling vapour
options.B: A vacuum pump — creating suction that draws the filtrate through the Buchner funnel
options.C: A burette for standardized delivery of acid
options.D: A thermometer to monitor the reaction temperature

questions.explanation: The side arm of the Buchner flask connects via rubber tubing to a vacuum pump. The reduced pressure inside pulls filtrate rapidly through the filter cake.

questions.stem: The separating funnel has a glass stopcock and is pear-shaped. What is it primarily used for?

options.A: Separating miscible liquids with closely related boiling points
options.B: Separating immiscible liquids (e.g. kerosene and water) that form two distinct density-based layers
options.C: Filtering fine solid particles out of a liquid suspension
options.D: Separating dissolved gases from a liquid mixture

questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids separate into layers by density in the separating funnel. The stopcock allows the lower (denser) layer to be drained first.

questions.stem: Why must a pipette filler be used instead of sucking a pipette with the mouth?

options.A: Because mouth suction gives less accurate volume measurements
options.B: Safety — the liquid may be toxic, corrosive, or harmful; the rubber filler prevents any contact with the mouth
options.C: Because the rubber filler maintains the liquid at constant temperature
options.D: Because mouth suction introduces CO₂ from breath, contaminating the solution

questions.explanation: Mouth pipetting is strictly forbidden in modern laboratories. The rubber bulb filler keeps hazardous liquids away from the mouth entirely.

questions.stem: A bulb (transfer) pipette is used during titrations. What is its primary function?

options.A: Dispensing indicator liquid dropwise during endpoint detection
options.B: Accurately transferring a fixed, definite volume (e.g. 25.00 cm³) of solution from a stock solution to the conical flask
options.C: Measuring approximate volumes in a large beaker
options.D: Filling the burette from the reagent bottle safely

questions.explanation: A bulb (one-mark) pipette delivers exactly one fixed volume with the highest accuracy (±0.04 cm³), far superior to measuring cylinders or beakers.

questions.stem: The Liebig condenser's function in distillation is to:

options.A: Increase the boiling point of the liquid being distilled
options.B: Cool and condense vapour from the flask into liquid distillate using cold water flowing through the outer jacket
options.C: Separate gases by molecular weight in a density gradient
options.D: Precisely measure the temperature of the boiling liquid

questions.explanation: The Liebig condenser uses flowing cold water in the outer jacket to cool and condense vapour passing through the inner tube, converting it back to liquid.

questions.stem: A Buchner funnel is made of perforated porcelain. When connected to a vacuum pump, what process does it enable?

options.A: Simple gravity filtration using folded filter paper
options.B: Fractional distillation of close-boiling liquid mixtures
options.C: Filtration under suction (reduced pressure), which is faster and leaves the solid drier
options.D: Intermittent supply of liquid acid reagents to a reaction mixture

questions.explanation: Vacuum filtration through a Buchner funnel is 10× faster than gravity filtration and produces much drier filter cakes — essential for collecting crystalline products.

questions.stem: Why is a round-bottomed flask (RBF) preferred over a flat-bottomed flask for distillation and reflux?

options.A: Because it is cheaper and more readily available
options.B: Because it holds more liquid than a flat-bottomed flask of the same size
options.C: Because the curved surface distributes heat evenly and prevents the glass from cracking under thermal stress
options.D: Because it can be stoppered more easily with a rubber bung

questions.explanation: Curved glassware distributes thermal stress evenly. Flat-bottomed flasks concentrate stress at corners and can crack when heated strongly.

questions.stem: A thistle funnel has a bulb top and long, narrow stem. What is it used for in gas preparation?

options.A: Filtering solid impurities from a liquid solvent
options.B: Adding a liquid reagent (acid) to a solid inside a flask, allowing controlled introduction while sealing the apparatus
options.C: Separating two immiscible liquid layers in an extraction
options.D: Dispensing a measured volume of indicator to a conical flask

questions.explanation: The thistle funnel allows addition of acid dropwise to the solid reactant while keeping the gas-generation apparatus sealed, controlling gas production rate.

questions.stem: In a titration set-up, why is a white tile placed beneath the conical flask?

options.A: To prevent the flask from sliding during swirling
options.B: To keep the flask and its contents warm
options.C: To provide a sharp, bright white background making the colour change at the endpoint easier to detect
options.D: To reflect heat from below and maintain a steady reaction temperature

questions.explanation: The white background maximises contrast at the titration endpoint, helping the analyst detect the precise moment of permanent colour change.

questions.stem: Which five pieces of apparatus are all used for measuring or delivering volumes of liquid?

options.A: Pipette, burette, measuring cylinder, volumetric flask, and graduated conical flask
options.B: Crucible, watch glass, petri dish, evaporating dish, and desiccator
options.C: Bunsen burner, retort stand, tripod, gauze, and crucible tongs
options.D: Separating funnel, thistle funnel, Buchner funnel, filter funnel, and dropper

questions.explanation: All volumetric glassware (pipette, burette, measuring cylinder, volumetric flask) measure or deliver liquid volumes. Each has a specific accuracy level for different applications.

questions.stem: Simple distillation separates components based on which physical property?

options.A: Difference in density of the two liquids
options.B: Difference in volatility (boiling point) — the more volatile component evaporates and is condensed first
options.C: Difference in solubility in a common third solvent
options.D: Difference in magnetic susceptibility of the components

questions.explanation: Simple distillation works best when boiling points differ by more than 25°C. The lower boiling point component distils over first.

questions.stem: Which method is used to separate a mixture of immiscible liquids such as kerosene and water?

options.A: Separating funnel — the two immiscible liquids form separate density-based layers
options.B: Evaporation — the water evaporates, leaving the kerosene
options.C: Filtration — using filter paper to trap the kerosene
options.D: Simple distillation — the liquids are boiled and condensed separately

questions.explanation: Kerosene (less dense, upper layer) and water (denser, lower layer) separate by density. The stopcock allows each layer to be drained independently.

questions.stem: Which separation method is used to separate several solutes that all dissolve in the same solvent?

options.A: Evaporation to dryness — removes only the solvent
options.B: Gravity filtration — separates only insoluble solids
options.C: Chromatography — different solutes migrate at different rates through the stationary phase
options.D: Sublimation — applicable only when one component sublimes

questions.explanation: Chromatography separates solutes based on their differential affinity for the stationary phase vs. the mobile phase, giving different migration distances (Rf values).

questions.stem: Which method of separation is used to separate butter from curd?

options.A: Sublimation — one component sublimes when gently heated
options.B: Paper chromatography — components travel at different rates
options.C: Centrifugation — rapid spinning separates the less-dense fat from the denser liquid
options.D: Magnetic separation — fat is non-magnetic

questions.explanation: Centrifugation uses centrifugal force to separate components of different densities. Butter (less dense fat) separates from curd (denser liquid).

questions.stem: In paper chromatography, the Rf value of a substance is defined as:

options.A: Distance moved by solvent front ÷ distance moved by spot from baseline
options.B: Mass of solute ÷ volume of solvent used
options.C: Distance moved by spot from baseline ÷ distance moved by solvent front from baseline
options.D: Distance moved by spot × concentration of the applied solution

questions.explanation: Rf = distance (spot) / distance (solvent front). It is always between 0 and 1, and is characteristic of the substance in a given solvent system.

questions.stem: Selection of the correct filter paper grade depends on:

options.A: The drying rate of the paper after filtration
options.B: Finer particles require slower, denser paper; coarser particles allow faster-flow paper
options.C: The ability of the paper to absorb and decolorise the solution
options.D: The paper's thickness to determine the decantation rate

questions.explanation: Filter paper pore size must match particle size. If pores are too large, fine particles pass through; if too small, filtration is too slow.

questions.stem: Fractional distillation of liquefied air separates nitrogen and oxygen because:

options.A: Nitrogen is magnetic and oxygen is not
options.B: They have different densities in the liquid phase
options.C: N₂ (b.p. −196°C) has a lower boiling point than O₂ (b.p. −183°C) and boils off first during gradual warming
options.D: They have different solubilities in the liquid nitrogen phase

questions.explanation: During gradual warming of liquid air, the more volatile nitrogen (lower b.p.) evaporates first and is collected separately from the less volatile oxygen.

questions.stem: Sublimation as a separation technique is applicable when:

options.A: Both components dissolve in the same solvent at room temperature
options.B: One component converts directly from solid to vapour without melting when gently heated, while the other remains solid
options.C: Both components are liquids with significantly different boiling points
options.D: One component is ferromagnetic and the other is non-magnetic

questions.explanation: Substances that sublime (e.g. iodine, ammonium chloride, naphthalene) can be separated from non-subliming impurities by gentle heating and condensation.

questions.stem: Zone refining (zone melting) is an advanced purification technique used to produce ultra-pure:

options.A: Distilled water for laboratory use
options.B: Semiconductor materials like silicon and germanium for the electronics industry
options.C: Salt (NaCl) from seawater by controlled crystallisation
options.D: Pharmaceutical compounds from plant extracts

questions.explanation: Zone refining sweeps impurities to one end of a solid rod by moving a narrow molten zone along it repeatedly, producing 99.9999% pure semiconductors.

questions.stem: Steam distillation is used to separate substances that:

options.A: Are completely miscible with water in all proportions
options.B: Are immiscible with water and have high boiling points — they co-distil with steam at temperatures below 100°C
options.C: Are solids that sublime readily when heated gently
options.D: Are gases at room temperature and must be liquefied for collection

questions.explanation: Steam distillation is used to isolate high-boiling, water-immiscible compounds (e.g. essential oils) without decomposing them at their normal boiling points.

questions.stem: In liquid-liquid extraction, the process depends on:

options.A: The difference in density between the two solvents
options.B: The partition coefficient — the ratio of solute concentration in solvent A to solvent B at equilibrium
options.C: The difference in boiling point between the two solvents
options.D: The magnetic susceptibility of the solute in each solvent

questions.explanation: The partition (distribution) coefficient K = [solute]_A / [solute]_B determines how completely a solute transfers between two immiscible solvents.

questions.stem: What is the stationary phase in paper chromatography?

options.A: The solvent (mobile phase) that moves up the paper
options.B: The water adsorbed on the cellulose fibres of the paper
options.C: The solute being separated and identified
options.D: The solvent front that moves to the top of the paper

questions.explanation: In paper chromatography, the cellulose paper fibres adsorb water, which acts as the stationary phase. The solvent (mobile phase) moves through it carrying solutes at different rates.

questions.stem: Which separation technique is dependent on difference in volatility?

options.A: Distillation
options.B: Crystallization
options.C: Magnetic separation
options.D: Fractional crystallization

questions.explanation: Distillation separates mixtures based on differences in boiling points (volatility). The more volatile component evaporates first and is condensed separately.

questions.stem: When is a buffer solution used in chemistry?

options.A: To make a solution permanently and strongly basic
options.B: To make a solution permanently and strongly acidic
options.C: To resist (prevent) significant changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
options.D: To neutralise all acids and bases to exactly pH 7.0

questions.explanation: A buffer solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, maintaining a relatively constant pH.

questions.stem: What type of indicator is Chlorophenol Red?

options.A: A redox indicator that changes colour with changes in oxidation state
options.B: A colorimetric (pH) indicator — changes colour based on the acidity or alkalinity of the solution
options.C: An adsorption indicator used in precipitation titrations
options.D: A radioactive tracer used in kinetic studies

questions.explanation: Chlorophenol Red is a pH colorimetric indicator that changes colour based on the hydrogen ion concentration of the solution.

questions.stem: Phenolsulfonphthalein (Phenol Red) appears what colour at exactly pH 7.0?

options.A: Bright red
options.B: Violet or purple
options.C: Blue-green
options.D: Yellow — it is yellow below pH 6.8 and transitions to red above pH 8.4

questions.explanation: Phenol Red appears yellow below pH 6.8, orange at neutral pH 7, and bright pink/red above pH 8.4.

questions.stem: Why does the [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ complex solution appear red?

options.A: It emits red light through fluorescence when excited by UV radiation
options.B: It absorbs green wavelengths (~490 nm) and transmits the complementary red wavelengths to our eyes
options.C: It absorbs all red wavelengths and reflects all green light
options.D: The SCN⁻ ion itself is inherently red-coloured in all metal complexes

questions.explanation: The Fe(SCN)²⁺ complex absorbs green light (complementary colour) and transmits red light, which is what we perceive as the red colour.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a reducing agent?

options.A: It accepts electrons from the substance it reacts with and is itself reduced
options.B: It has a higher oxidation state than the substance being reduced
options.C: It donates electrons to the oxidising agent, reducing it — and is itself oxidised in the process
options.D: It is always a metal oxide or a hydroxide compound

questions.explanation: A reducing agent donates electrons to other species (oxidising agents), causing them to be reduced. The reducing agent itself gets oxidised (loses electrons).

questions.stem: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) has a standard electrode potential of:

options.A: 0.00 V — by international convention
options.B: +2.87 V — the most positive possible electrode potential
options.C: −3.04 V — the most negative electrode potential
options.D: +1.23 V — the potential for oxygen evolution

questions.explanation: By international convention, the SHE is assigned E° = 0.00 V at all temperatures. All other standard electrode potentials are measured relative to it.

questions.stem: Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) is deep purple. When it reacts with a reducing agent in acidic solution, what colour change occurs?

options.A: Colourless to deep purple
options.B: Deep purple/violet to colourless (or very pale pink) — MnO₄⁻ reduced to Mn²⁺
options.C: Yellow to colourless — the chromate ion is reduced
options.D: Blue to red — the complex ion changes oxidation state

questions.explanation: MnO₄⁻ (purple, Mn in +7 state) is reduced to Mn²⁺ (almost colourless, pale pink) in acidic solution. The colour disappearance marks the endpoint.

questions.stem: With an increase in temperature, which concentration measure changes while others remain constant?

options.A: Molality (mol/kg) — based on mass of solvent
options.B: Mole fraction — a dimensionless ratio of moles
options.C: Molarity (mol/L) — volume changes with temperature, so mol/L changes too
options.D: Mass percent (% w/w) — based on mass ratio

questions.explanation: Molality, mole fraction, and mass fraction are temperature-independent (based on mass). Molarity depends on volume which changes with temperature.

questions.stem: Which indicator is used in EDTA complexometric titration for determining water hardness?

options.A: Phenolphthalein — colourless to pink at pH 9
options.B: Methyl orange — red to yellow in acidic to basic transition
options.C: Eriochrome Black T (EBT) — wine-red in presence of metal ions, turns blue at endpoint
options.D: Starch solution — gives a blue-black colour with iodine

questions.explanation: EBT forms a wine-red complex with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions. When EDTA fully complexes all metal ions, EBT is released and turns blue — this is the endpoint.

questions.stem: In an iodometric titration, starch indicator gives what endpoint?

options.A: Colourless to pink — starch reacts with iodide to form a coloured complex
options.B: Blue-black to colourless — starch forms blue-black complex with I₂; at endpoint all I₂ is consumed and colour disappears
options.C: Yellow to red — the iodo-starch complex changes colour as pH increases
options.D: Colourless to yellow — the appearance of free iodine causes the yellow colour

questions.explanation: Starch forms an intense blue-black complex with I₃⁻. When the reducing agent consumes all I₂, the blue-black colour disappears sharply — the endpoint.

questions.stem: When excess NaOH is added to a solution containing Cu²⁺ ions, what is observed?

options.A: A white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution
options.B: A green precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH
options.C: A pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ that is insoluble in excess NaOH
options.D: No precipitate — Cu²⁺ ions remain in solution even with excess NaOH

questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂↓ (pale blue gelatinous precipitate). This precipitate does NOT dissolve in excess NaOH, distinguishing Cu²⁺ from Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺.

questions.stem: When excess NaOH is added to a solution containing Al³⁺ ions, what is observed?

options.A: A pale blue gelatinous precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH
options.B: A green precipitate that darkens on standing in air
options.C: A white gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)₃ that dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless aluminate solution
options.D: No precipitate — Al³⁺ remains fully in solution even with excess NaOH

questions.explanation: Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric — it dissolves in excess NaOH: Al(OH)₃ + NaOH → NaAl(OH)₄ (sodium aluminate, colourless solution). This amphoteric behaviour distinguishes Al³⁺.

questions.stem: The 'brown ring' test is used to confirm the presence of which ion?

options.A: The sulphate ion (SO₄²⁻)
options.B: The nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) — FeSO₄ + conc. H₂SO₄ gives a brown ring at the interface
options.C: The chloride ion (Cl⁻)
options.D: The carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻)

questions.explanation: The brown ring test: FeSO₄ solution + test solution layered over conc. H₂SO₄. A brown ring of [Fe(NO)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ at the interface confirms NO₃⁻.

questions.stem: When AgNO₃ solution is added to a solution containing Cl⁻ ions, what is observed?

options.A: A yellow precipitate soluble in dilute HNO₃
options.B: A white precipitate of AgCl insoluble in dilute HNO₃ but soluble in dilute NH₃
options.C: A red precipitate of Ag₂CrO₄ insoluble in all acids
options.D: No precipitate — chloride ions remain in solution

questions.explanation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl↓ (white). AgCl is insoluble in dilute HNO₃ but dissolves in dilute NH₃: AgCl + 2NH₃ → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻. This confirms Cl⁻.

questions.stem: When dilute H₂SO₄ is added to a carbonate or bicarbonate, what is observed?

options.A: Yellow fumes produced that turn moist starch-iodide paper blue
options.B: Colourless odourless gas produced that turns limewater milky
options.C: A pungent smell of SO₂ and a white precipitate forms
options.D: Effervescence of a gas that relights a glowing splint

questions.explanation: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. CO₂ turns limewater (Ca(OH)₂ solution) milky due to CaCO₃ precipitation. This is the standard test for CO₃²⁻ and CO₂.

questions.stem: A gas that turns moist blue litmus paper red and has a pungent smell is most likely:

options.A: Ammonia (NH₃)
options.B: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
options.C: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) or sulphur dioxide (SO₂) — acidic pungent gases
options.D: Nitrogen (N₂)

questions.explanation: Acidic gases like HCl, SO₂, and HBr turn moist blue litmus red. Ammonia turns red litmus blue. CO₂ is acidic but not pungent. N₂ is inert.

questions.stem: When diluting a concentrated acid with water, what is the correct safe procedure?

options.A: Add water slowly to the concentrated acid with constant stirring
options.B: Always add acid slowly into water — never add water to acid (prevents violent, exothermic spattering)
options.C: Mix acid and water simultaneously in equal rapid portions
options.D: Pour acid into water quickly in the fume cupboard

questions.explanation: Adding water to acid concentrates the heat locally causing violent spattering. Adding acid to water disperses the heat safely in the large volume of water.

questions.stem: Where must all pungent, choking, or poisonous gases be prepared in the chemistry laboratory?

options.A: At an open bench near a large window for cross-ventilation
options.B: In a sealed glass container at the back of the laboratory
options.C: In the fume cupboard (fume hood) — its extraction fan safely removes toxic gases from the lab air
options.D: Outdoors in the open air next to the laboratory building

questions.explanation: All toxic, corrosive, and choking gases (Cl₂, HCl, SO₂, NH₃, Br₂ vapour) must be handled in the fume cupboard to protect the experimenter.

questions.stem: What Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is essential in the chemistry laboratory at all times?

options.A: Only a lab coat to protect clothing from spills
options.B: Only safety goggles to protect the eyes from splashes
options.C: Laboratory coat, safety goggles, and closed-toe shoes — at minimum; gloves when handling corrosive or toxic substances
options.D: No PPE is required for simple, room-temperature experiments

questions.explanation: The minimum PPE in any chemistry lab are lab coat (body protection), safety goggles (eye protection), and closed shoes (foot protection from spills and broken glass).

questions.stem: Which variety of glass is most commonly used for high-quality chemistry laboratory apparatus?

options.A: Pyrex (borosilicate glass) — low thermal expansion, high chemical resistance, withstands strong heating
options.B: Soda-lime glass (sodaglass) — the most chemically resistant and cheapest
options.C: Lead crystal glass — used for precision optical components
options.D: Polycarbonate — a synthetic transparent polymer for impact resistance

questions.explanation: Pyrex/borosilicate glass has very low thermal expansion coefficient (~3×10⁻⁶/°C vs 9×10⁻⁶/°C for soda-lime glass), making it resistant to thermal shock during heating.

questions.stem: Plastic apparatus (polythene, polypropene) has a significant limitation in the chemistry laboratory. What is it?

options.A: They are very expensive compared to glass and porcelain apparatus
options.B: They cannot withstand contact with dilute mineral acids or water
options.C: They are readily dissolved or swollen by organic solvents (e.g. acetone, CHCl₃, benzene)
options.D: They are opaque and cannot be used where colour changes must be observed

questions.explanation: Plastics like polythene and polypropylene are chemically resistant to aqueous acids and bases but are attacked or swollen by many organic solvents.

questions.stem: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is used as a drying agent for prepared gases. Which gas CANNOT be dried with conc. H₂SO₄?

options.A: Hydrogen (H₂)
options.B: Chlorine (Cl₂)
options.C: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
options.D: Ammonia (NH₃) — reacts with H₂SO₄ to form (NH₄)₂SO₄

questions.explanation: NH₃ is an alkaline gas. It reacts with H₂SO₄: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄. So it cannot be dried using conc. H₂SO₄. Use CaO or soda-lime for NH₃.

questions.stem: A Kipp's apparatus (gas generator) allows intermittent production of gas WITHOUT heating. What reaction does it use?

options.A: A solid reacts with a liquid (acid) at room temperature — e.g. marble chips + HCl → CO₂; Zn + H₂SO₄ → H₂
options.B: A liquid mixture is heated to boiling and vapour collected over water
options.C: Two liquids are electrolysed to produce gas at electrodes
options.D: A solid is strongly heated in air until it thermally decomposes

questions.explanation: Kipp's apparatus has three chambers. Opening the tap allows acid to contact the solid, producing gas on demand. Closing the tap stops the reaction automatically.

questions.stem: When a gas jar or test tube containing a dangerous chemical breaks in the laboratory, what is the FIRST action?

options.A: Continue the experiment and clean up after
options.B: Alert everyone in the lab immediately; evacuate if necessary; then clean up following COSHH procedures with gloves and protective equipment
options.C: Pour water on the spill to dilute and neutralise it
options.D: Leave the area and allow the chemical to evaporate naturally

questions.explanation: Safety first: alert others, ensure everyone is safe, evacuate if the spill is serious. Then clean up following proper COSHH procedures with appropriate PPE.

questions.stem: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds containing element(s) ________.

options.A: Both hydrogen and carbon only
options.B: Carbon only
options.C: Hydrogen only
options.D: Oxygen, hydrogen and carbon

questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons by definition contain ONLY hydrogen and carbon atoms. Examples include methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), and benzene (C₆H₆).

questions.stem: What is the general molecular formula for alkanes?

options.A: CₙH₂ₙ
options.B: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
options.C: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
options.D: CₙHₙ

questions.explanation: Alkanes follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is the number of carbon atoms. E.g. methane CH₄ (n=1), ethane C₂H₆ (n=2), propane C₃H₈ (n=3).

questions.stem: What type of reaction do alkanes typically undergo?

options.A: Addition reactions with bromine water
options.B: Electrophilic substitution with halogens in sunlight
options.C: Free radical substitution — UV light initiates halogenation
options.D: Nucleophilic addition with HBr

questions.explanation: Alkanes undergo free radical substitution with halogens in the presence of UV light or high temperature. E.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (photochlorination).

questions.stem: Which functional group is present in alcohols?

options.A: Carbonyl group (C=O)
options.B: Carboxyl group (-COOH)
options.C: Hydroxyl group (-OH)
options.D: Amino group (-NH₂)

questions.explanation: Alcohols are characterised by the hydroxyl (-OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon. E.g. methanol (CH₃OH), ethanol (C₂H₅OH).

questions.stem: What is produced when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄?

options.A: An aldehyde and water
options.B: An ester and water — this is esterification
options.C: A ketone and hydrogen gas
options.D: A salt and carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Esterification: Alcohol + Carboxylic acid ⇌ Ester + Water (with conc. H₂SO₄ as catalyst). E.g. CH₃OH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₂OH is:

options.A: Methanol
options.B: Ethanol
options.C: Propan-1-ol
options.D: Butan-1-ol

questions.explanation: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH has 3 carbon atoms (prop-), it is an alcohol (-ol), and the -OH is on carbon 1 (1-ol). Hence propan-1-ol.

questions.stem: 25 mL of barium hydroxide solution titrated against 0.1 M HCl gave titer of 35 mL. What is the molarity of Ba(OH)₂?
How many moles of NaOH are needed to neutralise 25 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄?

options.C: 0.01 mol

questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.025×0.1 = 0.0025 mol. Moles NaOH = 2×0.0025 = 0.005 mol.

questions.stem: What volume of 2 M HCl is needed to dissolve 5.85 g of NaCl? (Molar mass NaCl = 58.5 g/mol)

options.A: 50 mL
options.B: 100 mL
options.C: No HCl is needed — NaCl dissolves in water
options.D: 200 mL

questions.explanation: NaCl is a neutral salt that dissolves readily in water without needing acid. This question tests understanding that HCl is unnecessary for dissolving neutral salts.

questions.stem: The molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 4 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) in water to make 500 mL of solution is:
questions.explanation: Moles NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 500 mL = 0.5 L. Molarity = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 M.

questions.stem: The process in which the heavier impurities settle at the bottom is ____.

options.A: Decantation
options.B: Sedimentation
options.C: Filtration
options.D: Evaporation

questions.explanation: Sedimentation is the process where suspended particles settle to the bottom under gravity due to their higher density compared to the liquid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a method of separation used to separate a mixture that comprises solutes that dissolve in the same solvent?

options.A: Evaporation
options.B: Filtration
options.C: Chromatography
options.D: Sublimation

questions.explanation: Chromatography separates mixtures of solutes dissolved in the same solvent based on their different affinities for the stationary and mobile phases.

questions.stem: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds with element ________.

options.A: Both hydrogen and carbon
options.B: Carbon
options.C: Hydrogen
options.D: Oxygen

questions.explanation: Hydrocarbons by definition contain ONLY hydrogen and carbon atoms. Examples include methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), and benzene (C₆H₆).

questions.stem: What is the potential value of standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) at 298K?
questions.explanation: By international convention, the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is assigned a standard electrode potential of exactly 0 V at all temperatures.

questions.stem: In photosynthesis reaction water is oxidised into ____________.

options.A: H₂
options.B: CO₂
options.C: C₆H₁₂O₆
options.D: O₂

questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, water molecules are split (oxidised) by light energy: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂. The oxygen is released as a byproduct.

questions.stem: What is the correct statement for 'reducing agent'?

options.A: It has a higher oxidation state
options.B: It withdraws electrons
options.C: It reduces oxidising agents by donating electrons
options.D: It gets reduced itself in the redox reaction

questions.explanation: A reducing agent donates electrons to other species (oxidising agents), causing them to be reduced. The reducing agent itself gets oxidised.

questions.stem: 25 mL of a solution of barium hydroxide on titration with 0.1 molar solution of hydrochloric acid gave titer value of 35 mL. The molarity of barium hydroxide solution was:
When do we use Buffer Solution?

options.A: To make the solution basic
options.B: To make the solution acidic
options.C: To prevent solution's pH change
options.D: None of the above

questions.explanation: A buffer solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added, maintaining a relatively constant pH.

questions.stem: What is the colour of the Phenolsulfonphthalein indicator at pH 7.0?

options.A: Red
options.B: Violet
options.C: Green
options.D: Yellow

questions.explanation: Phenol Red (Phenolsulfonphthalein) appears yellow below pH 6.8, orange-red at neutral pH 7, and bright pink/red above pH 8.4.

questions.stem: Why does the colour of [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ solution appear red?

options.A: Complex add red radiation to solvent
options.B: Absorbs in the complementary green region and transmit red component
options.C: Absorbs in the red region
options.D: None of the above

questions.explanation: The Fe(SCN)²⁺ complex absorbs green light (complementary colour) and transmits red light, which is what we perceive as the red colour.

questions.stem: How is Oil and Hexane separated?

options.A: Distillation
options.B: Separating funnel
options.C: Crystallization
options.D: Electrophoresis

questions.explanation: Oil and hexane are immiscible liquids that form separate layers. A separating funnel allows the denser layer to be drained off independently.

questions.stem: Selection of filter paper depends on size of particles to be ________.

options.A: filtered
options.B: dried
options.C: decolorized
options.D: decanted

questions.explanation: Filter paper pore size is chosen based on the size of the particles to be filtered — coarser particles use larger pore size paper.

questions.stem: Which subatomic particle determines the atomic number of an element?

options.A: Neutron
options.B: Proton
options.C: Electron
options.D: Positron

questions.explanation: The atomic number (Z) equals the number of protons in the nucleus. It uniquely identifies an element and determines its position in the periodic table.

questions.stem: The mass number of an atom is defined as:

options.A: Number of protons only
options.B: Number of neutrons only
options.C: Number of protons + number of neutrons
options.D: Number of electrons + number of protons

questions.explanation: Mass number (A) = number of protons (Z) + number of neutrons (N). Electrons contribute negligible mass and are not included in the mass number.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of:

options.A: Electrons
options.B: Protons
options.C: Neutrons
options.D: Positrons

questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z, same number of protons) that differ in the number of neutrons, giving different mass numbers.

questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons that can occupy the second shell (n=2) is:
questions.explanation: The maximum electrons per shell = 2n². For n=2: 2×(2²) = 8. The second shell has 2 subshells: 2s (max 2 electrons) and 2p (max 6 electrons), total = 8.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an ionic bond?

options.A: Sharing of electron pairs between two atoms of similar electronegativity
options.B: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer
options.C: Attraction between a hydrogen atom and a highly electronegative atom
options.D: Delocalized electrons shared across a metallic lattice

questions.explanation: Ionic bonds form when a metal transfers one or more electrons to a non-metal, creating oppositely charged ions (cation and anion) that attract each other electrostatically.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of sodium (atomic number 11) is:
questions.explanation: Na (Z=11): 2 electrons fill shell 1, 8 fill shell 2, leaving 1 electron in shell 3. Configuration: 2, 8, 1 or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

questions.stem: Which group of the periodic table contains the alkali metals?

options.A: Group 0 (Group 18)
options.B: Group I (Group 1)
options.C: Group II (Group 2)
options.D: Group VII (Group 17)

questions.explanation: Group I (Group 1) contains the alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. They have one valence electron and readily lose it to form +1 cations.

questions.stem: Across a period from left to right in the periodic table, atomic radius:

options.A: Increases because more electrons are added
options.B: Decreases because nuclear charge increases while electron shielding stays roughly constant
options.C: Stays the same because electrons fill the same shell
options.D: First increases then decreases at the transition metals

questions.explanation: Across a period, protons increase (higher nuclear charge), pulling electrons closer to the nucleus. Shielding remains similar as electrons fill the same shell.

questions.stem: A covalent bond is formed by:

options.A: Transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal
options.B: Sharing of electron pairs between two atoms
options.C: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
options.D: Delocalized electrons in a metallic lattice

questions.explanation: Covalent bonds form when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, achieving a stable noble gas configuration. E.g. H₂, Cl₂, H₂O.

questions.stem: The shape of a water molecule (H₂O) is:

options.A: Linear — all atoms in a straight line
options.B: Trigonal planar — three bonds at 120°
options.C: V-shaped (bent) — due to two lone pairs repelling the bonding pairs
options.D: Tetrahedral — four equal bond angles of 109.5°

questions.explanation: H₂O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. The lone pairs repel more strongly, compressing the H-O-H bond angle to ~104.5°, giving a bent (V-shaped) molecule.

questions.stem: Which of the following molecules has a linear shape?

options.A: H₂O (water)
options.B: NH₃ (ammonia)
options.C: CO₂ (carbon dioxide)
options.D: CH₄ (methane)

questions.explanation: CO₂ has two double bonds and no lone pairs on the central carbon. The two bond pairs repel equally, giving a linear shape with a bond angle of 180°.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonding occurs between molecules that contain:

options.A: Any hydrogen atom and any other atom
options.B: A hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F — and a lone pair on another N, O, or F atom
options.C: Hydrogen and a metallic element only
options.D: Any two polar molecules with a dipole moment

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds form between the δ⁺ hydrogen on N-H, O-H, or F-H and the lone pair of electrons on N, O, or F of a neighbouring molecule.

questions.stem: Which property of water is explained by hydrogen bonding?

options.A: Its ability to dissolve ionic compounds
options.B: Its unusually high boiling point (100°C) for a molecule of its size
options.C: Its colourless and odourless nature
options.D: Its reaction with metals to produce hydrogen gas

questions.explanation: Without hydrogen bonding, water's b.p. would be about -80°C (like H₂S, -60°C). Hydrogen bonds require extra energy to break, giving water its anomalously high boiling point.

questions.stem: According to the Brønsted-Lowry theory, an acid is defined as:

options.A: A substance that produces OH⁻ ions in solution
options.B: A proton (H⁺) donor — it gives a proton to another substance
options.C: An electron pair acceptor (Lewis acid)
options.D: A substance with pH less than 5

questions.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. E.g. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (HCl donates H⁺, so it is an acid).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a neutral solution at 25°C?

options.D: It depends on the concentration of water

questions.explanation: At 25°C, pure water has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L. pH = -log[H⁺] = -log(10⁻⁷) = 7. Below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a strong acid?

options.A: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH)
options.B: Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
options.C: Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃)
options.D: Formic acid (HCOOH)

questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid — it fully dissociates in water: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻. Acetic, carbonic, and formic acids are weak acids that only partially dissociate.

questions.stem: The reaction between an acid and a metal carbonate produces:

options.A: A salt, hydrogen gas, and water
options.B: A salt, carbon dioxide gas, and water
options.C: A salt and hydrogen gas only
options.D: An oxide, carbon dioxide, and water

questions.explanation: Acid + Carbonate → Salt + CO₂ + H₂O. E.g. 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O. The CO₂ effervescence is a test for carbonates.

questions.stem: What is produced when sodium hydroxide (NaOH) reacts with sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?

options.A: Sodium sulphate and hydrogen
options.B: Sodium sulphate and water
options.C: Sodium hydrogen sulphate and water only
options.D: Sodium oxide and sulphurous acid

questions.explanation: NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O (neutralisation). With excess NaOH: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: An amphoteric substance is one that can:

options.A: React with both water and alcohol
options.B: Act as both an acid (proton donor) and a base (proton acceptor)
options.C: Dissolve in both polar and non-polar solvents
options.D: Form both ionic and covalent bonds

questions.explanation: Amphoteric substances react with both acids and bases. Examples: Al(OH)₃, Zn(OH)₂, water (H₂O), and amino acids.

questions.stem: The indicator methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. What colour does it show at its end point (pH ~4)?

options.A: Yellow
options.B: Red
options.C: Orange
options.D: Blue

questions.explanation: Methyl orange transitions from red (acid, pH < 3.1) through orange (at transition pH ~4) to yellow (alkali, pH > 4.4). The endpoint is orange.

questions.stem: If the enthalpy of products is lower than the enthalpy of reactants, the reaction is:

options.A: Endothermic
options.B: Exothermic
options.C: Isothermal
options.D: Catalytic

questions.explanation: A lower final enthalpy means energy was lost (given off) to the surroundings during the reaction. ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions.

questions.stem: What is the standard enthalpy of formation (ΔHf°) for an element in its standard state?

options.A: 100 kJ/mol
options.B: 1 kJ/mol
options.C: 0 kJ/mol
options.D: It varies depending on temperature

questions.explanation: By thermodynamic convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of any element in its most stable form at standard conditions is exactly zero.

questions.stem: Hess's Law states that:

options.A: The enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the pathway taken
options.B: The total enthalpy change is the same regardless of the route, as long as initial and final states are the same
options.C: Endothermic reactions cannot occur spontaneously
options.D: All combustion reactions release exactly the same amount of heat

questions.explanation: Hess's Law (conservation of energy): ΔH for a reaction is independent of the pathway. This allows calculation of ΔH for reactions that cannot be measured directly.

questions.stem: An endothermic reaction is one in which:

options.A: Heat is released to the surroundings and the products have lower energy than reactants
options.B: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings and the products have higher energy than reactants
options.C: The temperature of the reaction mixture rises during the reaction
options.D: No energy change occurs and ΔH = 0

questions.explanation: In endothermic reactions, ΔH is positive. Energy is absorbed from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down. E.g. dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an exothermic process?

options.A: Melting of ice (solid → liquid)
options.B: Evaporation of water (liquid → vapour)
options.C: Combustion of methane (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O)
options.D: Dissolution of ammonium chloride in water

questions.explanation: Combustion is always exothermic — it releases energy as heat and light. Melting and evaporation are endothermic (absorb energy to break intermolecular forces).

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.A: Temperature
options.B: Concentration of reactants
options.C: Presence of a catalyst
options.D: The standard electrode potential of the reaction

questions.explanation: Rate of reaction is affected by temperature, concentration, pressure (for gases), surface area, and catalysts. Standard electrode potential is a thermodynamic quantity, not a kinetic one.

questions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by:

options.A: Increasing the concentration of reactants
options.B: Providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
options.C: Increasing the temperature of the reaction mixture
options.D: Increasing the pressure of gaseous reactants

questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy (Ea). More molecules have enough energy to react, so the rate increases, but ΔH remains the same.

questions.stem: Increasing the temperature of a reaction generally increases the reaction rate because:

options.A: It decreases the activation energy required
options.B: It increases the frequency of collisions AND the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ Ea
options.C: It increases the concentration of reactants in solution
options.D: It changes the equilibrium constant K

questions.explanation: Higher temperature means more kinetic energy: molecules move faster (more frequent collisions) and more molecules exceed the activation energy threshold.

questions.stem: For a heterogeneous reaction (solid + solution), increasing the surface area of the solid:

options.A: Decreases the reaction rate by exposing fewer reactive sites
options.B: Increases the reaction rate by providing more collision sites per unit time
options.C: Has no effect on rate — only concentration matters
options.D: Changes the equilibrium position of the reaction

questions.explanation: Grinding a solid into powder greatly increases surface area, exposing more reactive particles to the solution and increasing the frequency of productive collisions.

questions.stem: During the electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid, what is produced at the cathode?

options.A: Oxygen gas
options.B: Sulphur dioxide gas
options.C: Hydrogen gas
options.D: Sulphate ions are discharged

questions.explanation: At the cathode (negative electrode), H⁺ ions are reduced: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. At the anode, water is oxidised: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that:

options.A: The mass of substance deposited is inversely proportional to the current
options.B: The mass of substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity (charge) passed
options.C: Equal volumes of different gases are always deposited at electrodes
options.D: The voltage required for electrolysis depends on the electrode material only

questions.explanation: Faraday's 1st law: m = (M × Q)/(n × F), where m = mass, M = molar mass, Q = charge, n = electron count, F = Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol).

questions.stem: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, oxidation occurs at the:

options.A: Cathode (positive electrode)
options.B: Anode (negative electrode)
options.C: Salt bridge
options.D: External circuit wire

questions.explanation: In a galvanic cell: oxidation (loss of electrons) occurs at the anode (negative). Reduction (gain of electrons) occurs at the cathode (positive). Electrons flow from anode to cathode externally.

questions.stem: The standard electrode potential of the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell is −0.76 V. What does the negative sign indicate?

options.A: Zinc is a weaker reducing agent than hydrogen
options.B: Zinc is a stronger reducing agent than hydrogen — it is more easily oxidised than H₂
options.C: The cell reaction is endothermic
options.D: Zinc cannot undergo electrolysis

questions.explanation: A negative E° means the half-cell has a greater tendency to be oxidised than the SHE. Zinc readily loses electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), making it a good reducing agent.

questions.stem: Avogadro's number (Avogadro's constant) is approximately:
questions.explanation: Avogadro's constant (Nₐ) = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. It is the number of atoms, molecules, or ions in one mole of a substance.

questions.stem: The molar mass of H₂SO₄ is: (H=1, S=32, O=16)

options.A: 64 g/mol
options.B: 80 g/mol
options.C: 96 g/mol
options.D: 98 g/mol

questions.stem: How many moles of atoms are in 24 g of carbon? (Ar of C = 12)

options.A: 0.5 mol
options.B: 1 mol
options.C: 2 mol
options.D: 24 mol

questions.explanation: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 24 ÷ 12 = 2 mol of carbon atoms.

questions.stem: The empirical formula of a compound is the:

options.A: Actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule
options.B: Simplest whole number ratio of atoms of each element present
options.C: Structural arrangement of atoms in the molecule
options.D: Total molecular weight of the compound

questions.explanation: The empirical formula shows the simplest ratio. E.g. glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has the empirical formula CH₂O (ratio 1:2:1).

questions.stem: What mass of water is produced when 4 g of hydrogen completely combusts in excess oxygen? (H=1, O=16)
questions.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Moles H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol. Moles H₂O = 2 mol. Mass H₂O = 2 × 18 = 36 g.

questions.stem: A 25.0 mL sample of 0.200 M NaOH requires 20.0 mL of HCl for complete neutralisation. What is the concentration of HCl?
questions.explanation: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1:1 ratio). Moles NaOH = 0.025 × 0.200 = 0.005 mol. Moles HCl = 0.005 mol. [HCl] = 0.005/0.020 = 0.250 M.

questions.stem: Boyle's Law states that, at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is:

options.A: Directly proportional to its volume
options.B: Inversely proportional to its volume (P ∝ 1/V)
options.C: Independent of its volume
options.D: Directly proportional to the square of its volume

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ at constant temperature. If volume doubles, pressure halves. Gas molecules spread further apart, hitting the walls less frequently.

questions.stem: Charles's Law states that, at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is:

options.A: Inversely proportional to the absolute temperature
options.B: Directly proportional to the absolute temperature (V ∝ T)
options.C: Independent of temperature
options.D: Proportional to the square root of temperature

questions.explanation: Charles's Law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ at constant pressure. As temperature rises, gas molecules move faster and occupy more volume. Temperature must be in Kelvin.

questions.stem: The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT. What does R represent?

options.A: Rate of reaction constant
options.B: The universal gas constant (8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
options.C: Ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium
options.D: Relative atomic mass of the gas

questions.explanation: R is the universal (molar) gas constant = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. It relates pressure, volume, moles, and temperature for ideal gases.

questions.stem: At standard temperature and pressure (STP), one mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately:
questions.explanation: At STP (0°C = 273.15 K, 1 atm), 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L (the molar volume). This is useful for gas stoichiometry calculations.

questions.stem: Graham's Law of diffusion states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is:

options.A: Directly proportional to its molecular mass
options.B: Directly proportional to the square root of its molecular mass
options.C: Inversely proportional to the square root of its molecular mass
options.D: Independent of molecular mass at constant temperature

questions.explanation: Graham's Law: rate ∝ 1/√M. Lighter gases diffuse faster. E.g. H₂ (M=2) diffuses 4× faster than O₂ (M=32) since √(32/2) = √16 = 4.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a colligative property?

options.A: Colour of the solution
options.B: Boiling point elevation
options.C: Conductivity of the solution
options.D: Viscosity of the solvent

questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not their identity. Examples: boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure, vapour pressure lowering.

questions.stem: Adding a non-volatile solute to a solvent causes the boiling point of the solution to:

options.A: Decrease — solute molecules lower the vapour pressure
options.B: Increase — solute molecules raise the boiling point above the pure solvent's boiling point
options.C: Remain unchanged — only the melting point changes
options.D: Depend on the identity of the solute

questions.explanation: Dissolved solute particles reduce the vapour pressure (Raoult's Law). The solution must be heated to a higher temperature before vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure — hence higher b.p.

questions.stem: Osmosis is defined as the movement of solvent molecules through a semi-permeable membrane:

options.A: From a region of high solute concentration to low solute concentration
options.B: From a region of low solute concentration (high solvent) to high solute concentration (low solvent)
options.C: Only from concentrated solution to dilute solution for ionic compounds
options.D: Against the concentration gradient using active transport

questions.explanation: Osmosis: solvent moves from dilute solution (high water potential) through a semi-permeable membrane to concentrated solution (low water potential).

questions.stem: Molarity is defined as:

options.A: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
options.B: Moles of solute per litre of solution
options.C: Grams of solute per 100 mL of solvent
options.D: Moles of solute per mole of solvent

questions.explanation: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres. E.g. dissolving 58.5 g NaCl (1 mol) in water to make 1 L gives 1 M NaCl solution.

questions.stem: Molality is defined as:

options.A: Moles of solute per litre of solution
options.B: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
options.C: Grams of solute per litre of solution
options.D: Moles of solvent per mole of solute

questions.explanation: Molality (m) = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg. Unlike molarity, molality is independent of temperature because it uses mass (not volume) of solvent.

questions.stem: What is the primary cause of acid rain?

options.A: Excess CO₂ in the atmosphere reacting with water vapour
options.B: Oxides of sulphur (SO₂, SO₃) and nitrogen (NO, NO₂) dissolving in rainwater to form H₂SO₄ and HNO₃
options.C: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) reacting with atmospheric water
options.D: Ozone (O₃) reacting with water droplets in clouds

questions.explanation: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃. These acids lower the pH of rain to below 5.6, causing acid rain.

questions.stem: The Haber process is used for the industrial synthesis of:

options.A: Sulphuric acid from SO₂ and O₂
options.B: Ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen
options.C: Nitric acid from ammonia and oxygen
options.D: Sodium hydroxide from sodium chloride by electrolysis

questions.explanation: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Conditions: 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst. About 150 million tonnes of NH₃ are produced annually for fertilisers.

questions.stem: Hard water is caused by the presence of dissolved:

options.A: NaCl and KCl — common table and potassium salts
options.B: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions from dissolved CaCO₃, CaSO₄, and MgSO₄
options.C: CO₂ gas dissolved from the atmosphere
options.D: Fe²⁺ ions from corroded pipes

questions.explanation: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions. These ions react with soap to form insoluble scum (metal stearates). They can be removed by ion exchange, boiling (temporary hardness), or adding Na₂CO₃.

questions.stem: What reagent is used to test for the presence of a C=C double bond (alkenes)?

options.A: Fehling's solution — turns from blue to brick-red precipitate
options.B: Bromine water — decolourised from orange/brown to colourless
options.C: Tollens' reagent — forms a silver mirror
options.D: Limewater — turns milky

questions.explanation: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with Br₂: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. Bromine water is decolourised instantly. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark.

questions.stem: Which reagent is used to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone?

options.A: Bromine water — decolourises with both
options.B: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) — gives silver mirror with aldehydes only
options.C: Concentrated H₂SO₄ — reacts with ketones only
options.D: Limewater — turns milky with aldehydes only

questions.explanation: Aldehydes are reducing agents and reduce Ag⁺ to Ag metal (silver mirror test). Ketones are not easily oxidised and give no reaction with Tollens' reagent.

questions.stem: Which gas is produced when a metal reacts with a dilute acid, and how is it tested?

options.A: CO₂ — turns limewater milky
options.B: O₂ — relights a glowing splint
options.C: H₂ — gives a squeaky pop with a burning splint
options.D: SO₂ — turns dichromate paper green

questions.explanation: Metals + dilute acid → salt + H₂. The squeaky pop test: a burning splint at the mouth of the test tube causes hydrogen to ignite with a characteristic 'pop'.

questions.stem: Limewater (Ca(OH)₂ solution) turns milky when which gas is passed through it?

options.A: Oxygen (O₂)
options.B: Hydrogen (H₂)
options.C: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
options.D: Nitrogen (N₂)

questions.explanation: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃↓ (white precipitate) + H₂O. The milky appearance is due to insoluble CaCO₃. Excess CO₂ redissolves the precipitate: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂.

questions.stem: How many molecules are in 0.5 mol of CO₂? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³)
questions.explanation: Number of molecules = moles × Nₐ = 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules of CO₂.

questions.stem: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ are produced from 6 moles of H₂?

options.A: 2 mol
options.B: 3 mol
options.C: 4 mol
options.D: 6 mol

questions.explanation: From the equation, 3 mol H₂ produces 2 mol NH₃. So 6 mol H₂ produces (6/3) × 2 = 4 mol NH₃.

questions.stem: Which of the following will NOT increase the rate of the reaction between marble chips and dilute HCl?

options.A: Increasing the temperature
options.B: Using powdered marble instead of chips
options.C: Adding more HCl to increase concentration
options.D: Adding a solid catalyst that is insoluble in HCl

questions.explanation: A catalyst that cannot contact the reactants (insoluble marble chips and aqueous HCl system) cannot lower the activation energy and therefore would not affect the rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following elements has the largest atomic radius in Period 3 of the periodic table?

options.A: Sodium (Na)
options.B: Silicon (Si)
options.C: Chlorine (Cl)
options.D: Argon (Ar)

questions.explanation: Across Period 3, atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl as nuclear charge increases. Na has the largest radius in Period 3 as it has the lowest nuclear charge (Z=11) pulling its outermost electron.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has the highest melting point?

options.A: NaCl (sodium chloride)
options.B: SiO₂ (silicon dioxide — giant covalent)
options.C: CO₂ (carbon dioxide)
options.D: H₂O (water)

questions.explanation: SiO₂ has a giant covalent lattice with millions of strong Si-O covalent bonds throughout — it requires very high energy to melt (~1650°C). NaCl has strong ionic bonds (~801°C). CO₂ is molecular and easily sublimes.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 M HCl solution? (HCl fully dissociates)
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 0.01 M = 10⁻² M. pH = -log[H⁺] = -log(10⁻²) = 2. This confirms that stronger acids (higher concentration) give lower pH values.
